summary: Describes the DDDS algorithm, which applies dynamically retrieved string transformation rules to an application-unique string. Well-formed rules reflect the delegation of management of the data tied to the string. It is part two of the DDDS series and replaces RFCs 2168 and 2915.

plainLanguage.summary: Follow the rules, change the string step by step, and end up at the right place. This is the exact step-by-step method DDDS uses.

subtitle: The loop that turns one string into an answer by repeatedly looking up and applying rewrite rules.

tldr.problem: Some identifiers, such as URNs, carry no network location, yet a client must still find the authority that holds data about them, even when that authority changes or delegates work to others.
tldr.mechanism: DDDS keeps rewrite rules in a database. A first well-known rule turns the Application Unique String into a key, the database returns rules for that key, and each rule is applied to the same original string until a terminal rule produces the final result.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3402 obsoletes RFC 2915 and RFC 2168. It defines only the general algorithm, so it is only useful together with an Application and a Database specified elsewhere in the DDDS series.

today: RFC 3402 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 2915 and RFC 2168, and it is read together with the other parts of the DDDS series starting with RFC 3401.

sections.title: What DDDS Is For
sections.content:
The Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) implements lazy binding of strings to data, to support dynamically configured delegation systems. It maps a unique string to data stored in a DDDS Database by iteratively applying string transformation rules until a terminal condition is reached.

The idea grew out of work by the Uniform Resource Name Working Group. URNs were designed to contain no information about network locations, yet clients wanted to find an authoritative server for one. The first system for this was called the Resolver Discovery Service and applied only to URNs. Later, other systems applied the same algorithm to non-URN problems, so the specifications were updated to allow new applications and rule databases to be defined in a standard way.

This document covers only the general algorithm. It is part two of a series specified in RFC 3401, and the RFC warns that no single document in the series can be understood without reading the others. It obsoletes RFC 2168 and RFC 2915 and updates RFC 2276.
sections.plainLanguage: Some names do not say where to find the thing they name. DDDS is a way to follow a trail of hints, one step at a time, until you reach the right place.

sections.title: The Vocabulary of DDDS
sections.content:
The RFC defines a small set of terms that the rest of the series reuses.

  • Application Unique String (AUS): the initial input. Its lexical structure must imply a unique delegation path.
  • Rewrite Rule: applied to the AUS to produce either a new key for the next lookup, or a final result string for the calling application.
  • First Well Known Rule: defined by the application, not stored in the database. It produces the first key.
  • Terminal Rule: a rule whose output is the final result rather than another key.
  • Application: the protocols and specifications that give actual values to the general parts of the algorithm.
  • Rule Database: any store where a unique key identifies a set of rules.
  • Services and Flags: fields in a rule that let the application choose between branches and recognise terminal rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of the starting word as your ticket, the rules as signposts, and the last signpost as the sign that says 'you have arrived'.

sections.title: The Algorithm Step by Step
sections.content:
Rules are collected in a DDDS Rule Database and fetched by key. A rule applied to the AUS yields a new key, which retrieves a new rule, which is applied to the AUS again, and so on until a terminating condition is reached. One constraint matters most: an application MUST NOT apply a rule to the output of a previous rule. Every rewrite rule is always applied to the exact AUS the process started with.

The exact algorithm has six steps:

  1. Apply the First Well Known Rule to the AUS to produce a key.
  2. Ask the database for the ordered set of rules bound to that key.
  3. Apply each rule's substitution expression, in order, to the AUS until one produces a non-empty string. If the list runs out with no match, tell the application that no valid output was available.
  4. If the rule's Service description does not meet the client's needs, go back to step 3 and continue down the list. Otherwise use this rule.
  5. If the rule's Flags say it is not terminal, go back to step 2 using the substitution result as the new key.
  6. Otherwise notify the application, giving it the Flags and Services of the rule and the output of the last substitution expression.

The algorithm assumes the information needed for each delegation decision is contained in the AUS and the rule itself. It does not handle decisions that depend on outside knowledge such as time of day, financial transactions or rights management.
sections.plainLanguage: You always read the same original word. Each clue tells you how to turn that word into the address of the next clue, and you stop when a clue says it is the last one.

sections.title: Rules and Substitution Expressions
sections.content:
A rule has four parts: a Priority (which of two otherwise equal rules takes precedence), a set of Flags (including whether the rule is terminal), a description of Services (semantic differences between delegation branches, such as load balancing, geographic segregation or backward-compatible behaviour for older clients), and a Substitution Expression.

The substitution expression combines a POSIX Extended Regular Expression with a replacement string, in the style of Unix sed. The first character of the expression is the delimiter, and there must be exactly three non-escaped occurrences of it. Digits MUST NOT be used as delimiters, because backrefs would be confused with literal digits. The only flag defined is i, for case-insensitive matching.

A backref \1 to \9 in the replacement is filled in with the text enclosed by the N'th pair of parentheses in the regular expression. The result must be a legal key for the database (or, for a terminal rule, valid output for the application), so clients SHOULD check that the result is a legal database key before using it.

Priority is only a preference between equivalent rules, so that some rules can act as fallbacks. The RFC states that it is not a load balancing mechanism, and applications that need load balancing should do it outside DDDS.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule is a little find-and-replace recipe. It looks for a pattern in your word and builds the next address from the pieces it finds.

sections.title: Specifying an Application and a Database
sections.content:
The algorithm is only useful when an Application and at least one Database are written down. An application specification must define the Application Unique String, the First Well Known Rule, the valid databases (and how the first key is made valid for each) and the expected output of a terminal rule. For example, the URI Resolution application defines the AUS to be a URI and could define the first key as the URI scheme, meaning the characters before the first colon.

No application may treat a key produced by a rule as the AUS for a new rule. The RFC says this leads to fragile, error-prone sendmail-style rewrite rules. The one exception is a flag that suspends the rules and hands control to something outside DDDS, such as the p flag in URI Resolution, which marks the next step as protocol specific.

A database specification must give a general specification (including character sets), a lookup procedure, a key format, a rule format, a rule insertion procedure and a rule collision avoidance method. Because several applications can share one database, such as ENUM and URI Resolution, collisions are avoided either by not allowing one key in two applications or by making the regular expression match enough of the AUS to tell the applications apart.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm is the game board. Each real use needs its own rulebook saying what the starting word looks like and where the clues are kept.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples, both explicitly made up and not based on any published application.

In the automobile parts example, a part number such as 4747301AB7D is the AUS. The first well known rule takes the first 5 digits, 47473, as the manufacturer ID and the key. The manufacturer's database returns a rule that uses the next 3 digits for a further query. In the example, 01A denotes the Toyota line, and the rule it returns delegates to a supply house in Japan and is marked terminal, so its result is the information about the part.

In the document identification example, the AUS looks like <organization>-<department>-<author>:<project>-<bookcase>-<book>, the database is an LDAP directory, and the first key is the characters before the first hyphen. Delegation can run all the way down to the author's own document management environment.
sections.plainLanguage: A part number is like a long address. The first piece sends you to the maker, the next piece sends you to the right factory, and the last clue gives you the answer.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the algorithm by itself implies no security issues. Real concerns can only be listed once the algorithm is combined with a particular Database and Application, but it notes that dynamic delegation points are a possible point of attack.

The document creates no requirements on IANA. Database and Application specifications may have considerable requirements, but they cannot be enumerated here.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the clues are fetched on the fly, someone could try to slip in a fake clue. The details depend on where the clues are stored, so each use has to check for that itself.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PARTS OF A DDDS RULE (RFC 3402)

items.title: Priority
items.text: Shows which of two otherwise equal rules takes precedence.

items.title: Flags
items.text: Mark attributes of the rule, including whether it is terminal.

items.title: Services
items.text: Describe features of a delegation branch so the client can choose.

items.title: Substitution Expression
items.text: A POSIX Extended Regular Expression plus a sed-style replacement.

viz.caption: SUBSTITUTION EXPRESSION GRAMMAR (ABNF FROM THE RFC)

data.title: subst-expr grammar
data.code:
subst-expr   = delim-char  ere  delim-char  repl  delim-char  *flags
delim-char   = "/" / "!" / <Any octet not in 'POS-DIGIT' or 'flags'>
ere          = <POSIX Extended Regular Expression>
repl         = *(string / backref)
string       = *(anychar / escapeddelim)
anychar      = <any character other than delim-char>
escapeddelim = "\" delim-char
backref      = "\" POS-DIGIT
flags        = "i"
POS-DIGIT    = "1" / "2" / "3" / "4" / "5" / "6" / "7" / "8" / "9"
